somalia.title: Somalia’s political future is at risk - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Somalia’s political future is at risk - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME OPINION Somalia’s political future is at risk Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Dr. Ali Said Faqi Thursday October 29, 2026 Somalia’s Third Republic was established as a federal country because no durable national government could be rebuilt through domination by the center. Federalism was intended to distribute power, accommodate regional interests and hold together a country fractured by decades of conflict. Today, that political settlement is under serious strain. Disputes over the Constitution, the electoral model and the division of authority have pushed the Federal Government of Somalia (FGS), several Federal Member States (FMS) and opposition groups toward confrontation. In Southwest State, that confrontation has become military. In this piece, I examine how disputes over federalism, constitutional amendments, the president’s expired mandate and the electoral process have brought Somalia to this point. I argue that the crisis cannot be resolved through unilateral decisions or force; it requires an inclusive political settlement that restores trust and keeps the national army out of partisan conflict. advertisements Puntland and Jubaland have rejected the federal government’s constitutional process, while other political actors accuse Villa Somalia of weakening the autonomy of the FMS and concentrating power in Mogadishu. The FGS argues that direct elections and stronger national institutions are necessary to move Somalia beyond repeated elite bargaining. That objective has merit. But a democratic system cannot gain legitimacy when one side determines the rules and imposes them on the rest of the country. The FGS’s approach toward the member states has therefore been interpreted as an attempt to dismantle federalism rather than reform it. The president points to voting conducted in parts of Southwest State, Galmudug and Hirshabelle as evidence that Somalia is advancing toward one-person, one-vote elections. Yet these processes were widely regarded by Somalis as selections rather than genuine elections. Political competition was restricted, outcomes were heavily managed, and voters were not offered a meaningful choice. Despite this, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has presented them as victories for democratization. Democracy cannot be measured by the opening of polling stations alone; it requires genuine competition, institutional independence and public confidence in the result. The electoral timetable has intensified the dispute as well. The president’s electoral commission has announced parliamentary elections for April 15, 2027, followed by a presidential election on May 15. Opposition groups reject the timetable because it was announced without agreement on the electoral framework, administration of the vote or constitutional basis for extending the current political arrangement. Much of the opposition supports direct elections in principle but disputes a process controlled by Villa Somalia. The unilateral timetable has also fueled rumors that the president intends to proceed with an election on his own terms, declare himself the winner and remain in office even if his authority is reduced to Villa Somalia. Whether or not this is his plan, the fact that such fears are circulating reflects the depth of mistrust and makes an agreed political process more urgent. That disagreement is also tied directly to the president’s mandate. Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s four-year term expired on May 15, 2026. In January 2024, he publicly assured Somalis that constitutional changes, particularly any change affecting the presidential term, would apply to the next legislative term, not the current one. Two months later, amendments were approved changing the terms of federal institutions from four to five years. The president now relies on those amendments to justify remaining in office until May 2027. His current position contradicts his earlier assurance. The opposition maintains that the amendments cannot be applied retroactively to extend a mandate obtained under the previous four-year arrangement. The president’s decision to proceed under the amended electoral model, including changes to how national leaders are elected, has deepened the constitutional crisis and damaged trust. The president is expected to uphold the Constitution and serve as a symbol of national unity, especially during a political crisis. His responsibility is to keep the country together while addressing competing national interests. When he becomes a party to the dispute rather than a credible mediator, the presidency loses its unifying role. The proposed consultative forum in Mogadishu from November 14 to 18 has not restored confidence. The invitation alone is insufficient, particularly after repeated failures to negotiate with opposition groups, even following international efforts to resolve the electoral disagreement. Many stakeholders suspect the invitation is intended to buy time rather than produce an agreement. That mistrust is reinforced by Villa Somalia’s failure to offer a clear agenda, agreed ground rules or a mutually accepted process for the dialogue. It has not explained how participants would shape the agenda or influence decisions already announced. Unless opposition concerns are addressed, the forum may not take place in any meaningful form. A meeting controlled entirely by the presidency would amount to political management, not negotiation. The political standoff is also playing out on the ground in Southwest State. In March, federal forces entered Baidoa, removed the administration of President Abdiaziz Laftagareen and supported a replacement authority. Armed confrontation has continued, with forces loyal to Laftagareen regaining several district centers and putting pressure on routes leading to Baidoa. The use of federal forces in this struggle has turned a political dispute into an internal armed conflict. That conflict is also diverting the Somali National Army from the national security role it is expected to assume as African Union forces draw down. The SNA is not ready to replace those forces across the country; some areas transferred to Somali forces have since returned to Al-Shabaab control. Using the army against domestic political opponents further weakens its ability to secure the country and undermines public confidence in its national mission. It also damages public confidence and creates opportunities for Al-Shabaab to expand. The continuing confrontation in Southwest State and the diversion of the SNA into internal political conflict make a negotiated settlement urgent. The immediate priority should be to de-escalate the fighting and keep the army out of partisan disputes. The president, FMS leaders and opposition groups should then enter negotiations under a process with a jointly agreed agenda and ground rules, with facilitation acceptable to all parties. Talks must address the disputed constitutional amendments, the president’s mandate and the electoral timetable, and produce a roadmap that all sides agree to respect. Without such an agreement, competing electoral processes, rival claims to legitimacy and further armed confrontation remain real risks. The central test is whether President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud will accept a negotiated electoral settlement that the federal member states and opposition can trust. Somalia’s political future depends on that choice. somalia.summary: Somalia's political future is increasingly precarious as tensions rise between the Federal Government of Somalia (FGS), Federal Member States (FMS), and opposition groups. Established as a federal system to distribute power and accommodate regional interests, the political framework is now under severe strain due to disputes over the Constitution, electoral processes, and the president's expired mandate. The situation has escalated into military confrontations, particularly in Southwest State, where federal forces have intervened. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's unilateral electoral timetable and constitutional amendments have deepened mistrust, as opposition groups fear he may attempt to extend his term without consensus. The proposed consultative forum in November has failed to restore confidence, with many viewing it as a tactic to delay meaningful negotiations. The ongoing conflict not only threatens political stability but also diverts the Somali National Army from its security role, exacerbating vulnerabilities to groups like Al-Shabaab. A negotiated settlement addressing these issues is urgently needed to secure Somalia's future.

somalia.content: The First Domino: Uganda's Withdrawal and the Unravelling of Somalia's Security Architecture - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Security Nationwide The First Domino: Uganda’s Withdrawal and the Unravelling of Somalia’s Security Architecture October 29, 2026 5 min read KAMPALA , Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia, Chief of Defence Forces General Muhoozi Kainerugaba announced, marking the first concrete step in a drawdown that comes just days after President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud asked Kampala to delay the departure from strategic locations in southern Somalia. In a post on X, Muhoozi said: “As we promised, we have started withdrawing UPDF from Somalia. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice we are handing over security to our Somali brothers.” The statement did not specify the number of troops involved, the locations affected, or whether the withdrawal would be conducted in phases. The announcement follows reports that President Mohamud had appealed to President Yoweri Museveni to delay the withdrawal from Barawe, Bulo Marer, Qoryoley, and Janaale, to allow Somali forces more time to prepare to take over security responsibilities. Whether the withdrawal has been adjusted to accommodate that request is not clear. The Funding Crisis Behind the Withdrawal Uganda’s decision is rooted in a funding crisis that has been building for months, and it is a direct consequence of the structural weaknesses documented in FTL Somalia’s analysis of Somalia’s $1 billion security bill . That analysis, drawing on the World Bank’s 2026 Public Finance Review, warned that the planned AUSSOM drawdown could force the government to assume costs it cannot afford or preside over a decline in security capacity as external funding recedes. The crisis deepened when the United States informed the African Union that it would not support extending the UN logistical support arrangement for AUSSOM beyond the current mandate, which expires on December 31, 2026. The UN Support Office in Somalia provides food, fuel, water, medical support, and casualty evacuation for the mission’s roughly 11,200 soldiers and 680 police officers. Without that support, AUSSOM’s operations become logistically untenable. As FTL Somalia reported, the UN support office has already begun preparing for liquidation, issuing a public tender seeking auctioneers to sell generators, medical equipment, prefabricated accommodation, and heavy machinery valued at approximately $30 million. The drawdown is no longer a threat. It is happening. Uganda’s Dual Role Uganda’s presence in Somalia has two tracks. Under AUSSOM, Uganda contributes approximately 4,500 troops to the multilateral mission. Separately, Uganda maintains a bilateral force of roughly 2,000 personnel under a security agreement signed with Mogadishu in late 2024. Muhoozi’s statement did not clarify whether the withdrawal affects the AUSSOM contingent, the bilateral force, or both. Uganda’s Defence Minister, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, said in August 2026 that Uganda would remain in Somalia even if the AU mission ended, citing the bilateral agreement. Muhoozi’s announcement appears to contradict that position, or at least to suggest that a full withdrawal is now the preferred course. The Security Gap The withdrawal will place additional pressure on the Somali National Army to take over positions currently secured by Ugandan forces, including areas around Mogadishu and its approaches where Al-Shabaab has repeatedly carried out attacks. Ugandan troops have been instrumental in protecting critical government facilities, including Aden Adde International Airport and Mogadishu Port. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Entebbe meeting , President Mohamud’s request for Ugandan troops to stay longer was a tacit acknowledgment that Somali forces are not yet ready to assume full security responsibility. Muhoozi’s announcement suggests that Uganda is proceeding with the withdrawal regardless, or at least beginning a process that will be difficult to reverse. The structural weakness of the Somali security sector is not new. As documented in FTL Dhambaal’s 2021 report, “AMISOM: A Rescue Mission in Need of Rescue” , the mission originally scoped for 8,000 troops and six months grew into a 20,000-person operation spanning every federal member state. The report warned that troop-contributing countries had developed elaborate systems for deducting from soldiers’ allowances, and that the AU mission had expanded far beyond its agreed strategic locations. The current withdrawal is the latest chapter in a long history of external actors deciding when and how to leave, while the Somali state struggles to build the capacity to secure itself. Critical Note Muhoozi’s announcement is a social media post, not a formal military order, and it lacks the operational detail that a withdrawal of this significance requires. It does not say how many troops are leaving, from which bases, or whether the bilateral force will remain. It does not address President Mohamud’s request for a delay. And it does not explain how the handover will be managed without creating gaps that Al-Shabaab can exploit. The broader context is one of a mission unravelling under financial pressure. The United States has withdrawn its support for the logistics that sustain AUSSOM. The European Union has reduced its funding. The African Union owes months of arrears to troop-contributing countries. Uganda is the first major contributor to act on the warnings it has been issuing for months. Others may follow. For Somalia, the message is stark. The international scaffolding that has supported its security for two decades is being dismantled, and the withdrawal is beginning before the Somali National Army is ready to stand on its own. Muhoozi’s words, “handing over security to our Somali brothers,” frame the withdrawal as a transfer of responsibility. Whether it becomes a transfer or an abandonment will depend on what happens in the weeks and months ahead, and on whether the Somali government can fill the gap that Uganda is leaving behind. The Dhambaal’s warning from 2021, that the “African solutions to African problems” narrative is crippled, has never been more relevant. The ministry identified the vessels as TCG Gökçeada and TCG Yıldırım but did not disclose the quantity or type of military equipment being transported. advertisements It also did not specify whether the supplies were intended for the Somali National Armed Forces or Turkish military personnel stationed in Somalia. The ministry did not announce when the warships were expected to arrive or how long they would remain in Somali waters. The announcement follows a meeting on Oct. 24 between the commander of the Turkish Land Forces and his Somali counterpart, who was accompanied by a military delegation. According to the Turkish Defence Ministry, the discussions focused on strengthening bilateral cooperation in defence, military training and security. Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to continuing military cooperation aimed at improving the capabilities of Somalia’s armed forces and contributing to regional security and stability. Turkey is one of Somalia’s key military partners, providing training, equipment and technical assistance to Somali security forces. Ankara operates a major military training facility in Mogadishu, where Turkish instructors have trained Somali soldiers as part of efforts to strengthen the country’s defence capabilities. The two countries have also expanded their military relationship through defence and maritime security agreements aimed at improving Somalia’s capacity to protect its territorial waters and combat security threats. The planned deployment of the two warships comes as Somalia and Turkey continue to deepen their military partnership, including cooperation on training, maritime security and defence capacity-building. Somali security forces intervened in September to recover the vessel, resulting in tragic consequences. Five crew members lost their lives during the operation, compounding the crisis. This comes after several years of efforts by international navies to suppress acts of piracy along the coast of Somalia. The seizure of the Honour 25 clearly demonstrates the dangers that accompany such situations. The oil tanker was heading to Somalia when gunmen seized control of the ship and took the 17-member crew hostage on April 21, 2026. The crew was held hostage for several months as efforts were made for their release. However, while Somali security personnel attempted to liberate the vessel in September, five members of the crew lost their lives. This assault has once again raised the issue of the possible return of piracy in Somalia against the backdrop of the Iranian war affecting maritime activity and military focus on other waters. CNN's article focuses on the issue of how changing priorities in security, valuable cargo, and the possibility of making money through ransom might provide pirates with new opportunities for an attack. Live Events An ordinary voyage turned into a five-month hostage ordeal The Honour 25 was transporting about 2,700 tonnes of diesel oil from Oman to Mogadishu, the capital city of Somalia, when the attack by the pirates occurred. In accordance with CNN reports, Syed Hussain Yousuf, second engineer on board, received an alert regarding the possible pirate attack prior to the gunfire being opened. Within minutes, armed individuals got on board and ordered the crew members to assemble on the bridge. The Honour 25 had seventeen crew members on board. Most of the time, the sailors were confined to the bridge, which is described as a very small area where the crew members had to stay seated and move around only if led by the kidnappers for toilet use. Yasir Khan, the chief engineer aboard the ship, survived after being shot in the leg. In an interview with CNN, he mentioned that there was no warning system, no security guards, and no other safety precautions against piracy. He also noted that the ship's engines and generators were in poor shape. The pirates demanded a multi-million-dollar ransom for the release of the ship. The negotiations were ongoing when the crew was held hostage, but the crisis was resolved by a security operation conducted on September 29. According to the Somali authorities, five people among the crew were killed before the ship. There have been some conflicting reports about how they died. Why Somali pirates are returning to the high seas Piracy in Somalia had become a serious menace to international shipping in the last years of the decade between 2000 and 2010. There had been attacks where gangs hijacked cargo ships and took their crews hostage, and it led to the disruption of shipping through the western part of the Indian Ocean. The reduction in such attacks was not because the factors that fostered the act ceased to exist. CNN noted that economic instability in Somalia, together with new openings arising from the Iran war, has encouraged pirates to attack vessels again. The war has made the military concentrate on the Persian Gulf and the Bab el-Mandeb strait due to the Houthis' attacks on commercial vessels. According to CNN, there is less military presence around Somalia due to the shift of the US military's attention to the region. The conflict has also led to increased prices for oil. The tankers loaded with oil provide the possibility of collecting money as a ransom from pirates, which makes them attractive targets. Honour 25 is not the only ship involved in the wave. According to CNN, there have been cases when six ships were seized at once at some point during the summer, with about 90 crew members in captivity. Another organisation has voiced its worries over the results of the hijacking: the International Maritime Organization. According to information from October, 44 seafarers were released from three ships, including Honour 25, with five of them perishing during the rescue operations. How piracy threatens shipping costs far beyond Somalia Beyond those who are confronted at gunpoint, there is the risk to the shipping process, which may be disturbed and made more costly because ships will need to reroute to navigate the seas safely. According to CNN, rising insurance premiums have followed from increased security risks for ships in transit. In some cases, ships have needed to travel via Africa to avoid perilous waters and have incurred additional costs in fuel and time to do so. These costs may eventually make their way to consumers, since oil and other products rely on shipping systems and additional costs of transport and insurance could increase delivery fees. There may be vulnerabilities of smaller firms. In this case, CNN reported concerns regarding ships that do not have the same security measures as larger ships. As far as the Honour 25 ship is concerned, there was no security on board when the pirates boarded the ship. Piracy is, therefore, more than just a story about armed men boarding commercial vessels. Piracy is about the vulnerability of the vessel, the funds that can be raised through ransom and the abilities of international security forces to ensure that the major shipping routes remain safe. The recovery of the Honour 25 meant an end to a long period of imprisonment, but it took a very high price to pay. As the war in Iran affects the security of the seas and the economics of seafaring, the resurgence of piracy is another problem that needs to be addressed. somalia.summary: Modern piracy off the coast of Somalia has resurfaced, with armed Somali raiders hijacking oil tankers and holding crews hostage for ransom. A recent incident involved the Honour 25, a diesel tanker seized on April 21, 2026, while transporting fuel to Mogadishu. The crew of 17 was held captive for several months, leading to a tragic rescue attempt in September that resulted in the deaths of five crew members. Despite international efforts to combat piracy, economic instability in Somalia and shifting military focus due to the Iranian conflict have created new opportunities for pirates. The resurgence of piracy not only threatens the safety of seafarers but also disrupts global shipping routes, leading to increased costs for shipping and insurance that could ultimately impact consumers. The Honour 25 incident highlights the ongoing vulnerabilities in maritime security and the complex factors contributing to the return of piracy in the region.

somalia.content: Somali piracy surges as Iran war diverts US naval attention - CNN | Iran International العربية فارسی Iran Insight Politics Economy Analysis Special Report Opinion Podcast Live TV Iran Insight Politics Economy Analysis Special Report Opinion Podcast Live TV Theme Language العربية فارسی Iran Insight Politics Economy Analysis Special Report Opinion Podcast Live TV All rights reserved for Volant Media UK Limited Latest News Somali piracy surges as Iran war diverts US naval attention - CNN Oct 29, 2026, 17:05 GMT+0 Listen to this article Share Pirates leave the merchant vessel MV Faina (not shown) for the Somali shore, while under observation by a U.S. Navy ship, October 8, 2008 Piracy off Somalia has reached its highest level since 2013, CNN reported Thursday, as maritime security experts warned that the Iran war and Houthi attacks on shipping were creating new opportunities for pirates. At one point this summer, six vessels were simultaneously held by pirates, with 90 crew members taken hostage, according to the European Union's Operation Atalanta naval mission. The resurgence has led to several major hijackings, including the MT Eureka oil tanker and the Honour 25 diesel tanker, whose crew remained captive for more than five months. Maritime security experts cited by CNN linked the increase to the diversion of naval resources toward the Persian Gulf and Bab al-Mandeb Strait, as well as rising fuel prices and economic hardship in Somalia. Houthi attacks have also pushed some commercial vessels closer to Somalia's coast, exposing them to greater risks. "As long as Iran and the Houthis continue to threaten maritime commerce, America and its regional partners will remain primarily focused on those threats, allowing piracy to flourish," Matthew Reisener, a senior national security adviser at the Center for Maritime Strategy, told CNN. The Honour 25, carrying 2,700 tons of diesel from Oman to Somalia, was hijacked in April, with its 17 crew members held captive for more than five months. Pirates initially demanded $7 million in ransom, later reducing the amount to $1 million, according to survivors interviewed by CNN. Five crew members were killed in late September during an operation by Puntland maritime police to free the vessel. Tim Walker, maritime project leader at the Institute for Security Studies Africa, said ships without armed guards were particularly vulnerable, while rising ransom demands had made piracy more profitable. "It's more lucrative to attack now," Walker said. "For one activity, pirates can get a very large payout – even a couple million dollars." Experts also pointed to worsening poverty, drought and rising food and fuel costs in Somalia as factors encouraging piracy. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appeared set to remain in power after Tuesday’s election left his opponents short of the seats needed to unseat him, as he raised the prospect of renewed military action against Iran alongside the United States. With nearly all votes counted on Wednesday, projections by Israel’s three main broadcasters gave Netanyahu’s bloc of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, against 48 for the opposition led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Arab parties were projected to win a record 19 seats. Neither bloc secured a majority, but the opposition's weaker-than-expected performance left Eisenkot with little prospect of forming a government without support from Arab parties, an arrangement many Jewish political leaders oppose. Netanyahu is therefore likely to remain caretaker prime minister while coalition negotiations proceed or until another election is held. President Isaac Herzog has said that Israel must avoid heading to the polls again after Tuesday’s vote. “We need to do everything, certainly after yesterday, so as not to hold another election,” he said. ‘Once and for all’ Addressing supporters in Jerusalem early Wednesday, Netanyahu called for a “strong, right-wing national government” and highlighted Israel’s military successes, including its operations against Iran. “Israel faces a singular historical opportunity, together with our partner President Trump, to remove the existential threat of Iran once and for all. But ulterior motives must not divert us from this sacred mission,” he said. His remarks raised the prospect of renewed joint military action against Tehran at a time of heightened tensions and diplomatic efforts to avert another round of fighting. Trump, who had urged Israelis to reelect Netanyahu so the two leaders could “finish the job” in Iran, praised his performance and credited his own endorsement. “It might be winning or tie. The tie is sort of considered a win in that case because it's a big chess match,” Trump said Wednesday during a campaign stop in Texas. Eisenkot, meanwhile, acknowledged that Netanyahu would remain in office as a caretaker but argued that the prime minister had lost public support and should retire from politics. He also warned security and civil service officials against allowing Netanyahu to use national security for political purposes. “Remember that you serve only the state and the interests of Israel's citizens. Stand firm in the face of any attempt to challenge you,” Eisenkot said. “Netanyahu, do not dare use Israel’s security for your political needs.” Turnout reached 77.7%, the highest in more than two decades, with particularly strong participation among Arab voters. Their parties' projected gains could give them an unusually influential role in determining whether an alternative government can be formed. Two charged over alleged Iran intelligence operation at RAF Fairford Oct 27, 2026, 17:44 GMT+0 Listen to this article 100 % A B-1B Lancer bomber arrives at RAF Fairford airbase, after police declared a major incident at the base and arrested several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act, who have since been released on bail, in Fairford, Gloucestershire, Britain, September 29, 2026. Two men appeared in a London court on Tuesday over an incident at a British air base used by US bombers to strike Iran, with prosecutors alleging that one of them sought to assist Iranian intelligence. British national Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, a 24-year-old dual British-Iranian national, appeared at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on charges under Britain's National Security Act. RAF Fairford in southwest England had been used by US bombers carrying out strikes on Iran. The aircraft were withdrawn on security grounds shortly after five British men were arrested outside the base in the early hours of September 27. Prosecutors said Abdulkarim arranged for five men to travel to the base in three vans at the request of a man identified only as “Ali.” The group bought around £300 ($400) worth of petrol and stored it in drums, prosecutor Louise Gray told the court. “One of them was told there was a bomb in the van,” Gray said. One of the men then called the emergency services, prompting police to arrive. Abdulkarim, who appeared in court in a wheelchair, is charged with engaging in conduct likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service between August 31 and September 28. Reconnaissance of US-used base Essghir was first arrested outside RAF Fairford on September 27 and is accused of entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the United Kingdom on August 22. Prosecutors said he had carried out reconnaissance of the base in August on instructions from “Ali” and was also in one of the vans that returned to Fairford the following month. After the men were told there was a bomb in the van, Essghir messaged “Ali” asking “wtf (what the fuck) is going on,” Gray said. He received no reply. The circumstances surrounding the September incident have remained largely unexplained and attracted international attention amid heightened concerns about the security repercussions of the US-Iran war for Western countries. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier this month that the activity at RAF Fairford was likely coordinated in Iran. Tehran's ambassador to Britain denied the allegation. Abdulkarim was granted bail and is due to appear in court again in November, while Essghir was remanded in custody. Police said six other people remain on bail, including four British nationals arrested outside RAF Fairford on September 27. The decision to release suspects on bail following the incident had drawn scrutiny. Police said on Tuesday that doing so had helped investigators secure the charges against Abdulkarim and Essghir. Israeli exit polls point to deadlock after Iran-dominated election Oct 27, 2026, 13:55 GMT+0 Listen to this article 100 % An advert for an Israeli television channel that will broadcast Israel's election coverage features Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, ahead of Israel's national election, on a bridge in Tel Aviv, Israel, October 21, 2026. Voting in Israel's election was drawing to a close Tuesday, with Iran a central issue and turnout reaching its highest level at this stage since 1988. Early exit polls in Israel's parliamentary elections on Tuesday pointed to a divided Knesset, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition nor the opposition securing enough seats to form a majority on its own. Projections by Israel's Channels 12 and 13 showed the two blocs closely matched, with Arab parties collectively holding a potentially decisive number of seats in the 120-member parliament. Channel 12 projected 52 seats for the opposition bloc, 50 for Netanyahu's bloc and 18 for Arab parties. Channel 13 put the opposition at 53 seats, Netanyahu's bloc at 50 and Arab parties at 17. Both projections left the main blocs short of the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority. The exit polls are preliminary and could change as votes are counted. Record vote “We have surpassed all the records kept by the Central Elections Committee,” acting director general Dean Livne said. “There hasn’t been such a nationwide voter turnout since 1973.” Long lines prompted election officials to say polling stations would remain open beyond their scheduled 10 p.m. closing time if voters were still waiting. “We promise, everyone will vote,” Livne said. “If there is a line at 10 p.m., the polling stations will continue to operate until everyone who arrived by 10 p.m. has voted.” Iran factor Iran has featured prominently in the closing days of the campaign. Israeli media reported that Netanyahu clashed with military chief Eyal Zamir over proposed action related to Iran that Zamir feared could trigger renewed conflict. Netanyahu denied the reports, while Defense Minister Israel Katz called reports of a rift baseless. Eisenkot backed Zamir, accusing Netanyahu of putting his political survival ahead of national security and warning that he would not allow the military to become a tool in Netanyahu’s “campaign of survival.” Another opposition leader, Avigdor Liberman, went further, saying any attempt to drag Israel into military action to prevent the election would amount to treason. Eisenkot, like Netanyahu, says Iran must be prevented from acquiring nuclear weapons and has backed military strikes against its nuclear program. But he has rejected Netanyahu’s pursuit of regime change in Tehran as an achievable military objective and argued for combining economic pressure and diplomacy with military action when necessary. Earlier this month, Eisenkot said another attack would be justified if Iran were making a dash for a nuclear weapon, but said he was unaware of any development requiring an immediate strike. The result is being followed closely in Iran, where Israel’s next government will inherit decisions over whether and under what circumstances to resume military action against Tehran. Mecca defense pact members hold talks with Iran Oct 26, 2026, 09:56 GMT+0 Listen to this article 100 % Officials from Iran, Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia attend a four-way meeting in Tehran on October 26, 2026. Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey opened talks with Iranian authorities in Tehran on Monday, following increased Iran-backed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and renewed warnings of military action between Tehran and Washington. Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin will travel to Tehran, Reuters reported on Monday, citing Saudi and Iranian officials. Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, confirmed the visit. The initiative was proposed during Munir's visit to Tehran last week, when he met President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials, according to a senior Iranian official. Iranian media reported that officials told Munir they would not negotiate with Washington until Tehran's demands were met. Defense pact faces first major test The visit marks the first high-level meeting between Iran and all three members of the Mecca defense pact since the escalation of hostilities. Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed the agreement in August, establishing that a military attack on one member would be considered an attack on all three. Pakistan has ratified the pact, while ratification remains pending in Turkey's parliament. Mecca pact ties three Sunni powers together as Iran-backed attacks loom Earlier this month, the three countries agreed to implement their defense commitments and rapidly deploy military personnel and capabilities to Saudi Arabia. The agreement faces its first significant test following increased Houthi attacks on Saudi territory. Saudi Arabia announced on Sunday that it had intercepted another wave of missiles and drones. The visit is intended to reduce hostilities and support mediation efforts by Qatar and Pakistan, Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister for Public Diplomacy Raed bin Khalid Qarmali said earlier. US-Iran confrontation Qatari officials also visited Tehran on Sunday for talks with Iranian authorities. Qatar pushes for Iran deal, new US strikes remain possible Previous mediation by Qatar and Pakistan helped secure a temporary halt to hostilities, but the agreement collapsed when fighting resumed. Indirect contacts between Tehran and Washington have continued through both mediators, a process also referenced by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. US President Donald Trump raised the possibility of renewed military operations against Iran on Friday. US and Iran trade new threats as diplomacy yields no breakthrough Iranian officials have warned that any further attack would trigger a stronger response. The diplomatic meetings come as Saudi Arabia seeks to prevent the conflict from spreading to its critical infrastructure, putting the Mecca defense pact and regional mediation efforts under growing pressure. Iran’s evasion network survives, but the crude feeding it has run dry Oct 23, 2026, 16:18 GMT+1 • Umud Shokri Listen to this article 100 % File photo: A worker stands on the Soroush offshore oil platform in Iran’s Persian Gulf Iran still has the knowhow, middlemen and shadow-fleet infrastructure it spent years developing to sell sanctioned oil to China. But it has now run out of oil outside Iran to put through that system. The US naval blockade has exposed a limitation in Tehran’s sanctions-evasion machinery: ship-to-ship transfers, false paperwork and steep discounts can disguise and sell crude once it is at sea, but they cannot get fresh cargoes out of Iranian ports. For months, Iran was able to keep selling oil to China because millions of barrels had already left the country on tankers and were sitting in Asian waters. That reserve is now effectively exhausted. Kpler analysts cited by The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday estimated Iran had about 135 million barrels in overseas storage when the war began in February. By October 5, that had fallen below one million barrels. Vortexa gave a different figure, estimating Iranian stocks off Singapore at roughly six million barrels on October 9. The difference reflects varying tracking methods and locations, but both show that the offshore stocks that sustained Iranian exports have been largely depleted. The Malaysia route dries up Malaysia sits at the heart of how Iranian oil has reached China, serving mainly as a transfer point rather than the true source of much of the crude. The Wall Street Journal reported in May on ship-to-ship transfers of Iranian crude off the Malaysian coast. A sharp drop in China’s purchases recorded as Malaysian crude could therefore provide another indication that the flow of Iranian oil through the system has dried up. But the figures are not a one-for-one measure of Iranian exports. Chinese customs data record the declared origin of cargoes, while ship tracking can miss transfers or vessels operating without transponders. The timing nevertheless coincides with the depletion of the offshore stocks that had fed the trade. If no new Iranian crude is available for transfer near Malaysia, fewer cargoes would be expected to appear in Chinese data under a Malaysian origin. China turns to other suppliers China remains Iran’s most important potential buyer, but its independent refineries are already lining up alternatives. Reuters reported on October 6 that Chinese “teapot” refineries had purchased at least 12 million barrels of Iraqi and Qatari crude for delivery in October and November. Traders suggested the total could reach 15 million to 20 million barrels. Iranian oil had been attractive largely because of its steep discount. Iraqi and Qatari cargoes may cost more, but they arrive through normal channels and carry less risk of sanctions trouble or sudden interruptions. Iran could offer deeper discounts or rely more heavily on intermediaries to retain Chinese customers. Neither solves the central obstacle: the oil still has to be loaded and shipped. Reuters reported in August that offers of Iranian oil to Chinese buyers had already fallen as stored cargoes were sold. Few alternatives to tankers Jask, on the Gulf of Oman, is often cited as Iran’s alternative export outlet. The Goreh–Jask pipeline and terminal were built so oil could reach the sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. So far, however, the facility has not shown it can replace Iran’s main export system. The International Energy Agency’s February 2026 factsheet described Jask as effectively out of regular service. S&P Global later reported tanker activity there between March and July, indicating occasional use. البرامج دول الهلال السوداني يصدم جماهيره بخسارة قاسية في الدوري الرواندي من خسارة الهلال أمام مارين الرواندي (Facebook/Al Hilal S.C) 28 أكتوبر 2026 الهلال السوداني يصدم جماهيره بخسارة قاسية في الدوري الرواندي الهلال السوداني الدوري السوداني الممتاز كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' تعرّض فريق الهلال السوداني لخسارة قاسية بنتيجة 0-3 أمام فريق مارين، في المباراة التي جرت اليوم الأربعاء 28 أكتوبر/ تشرين الأول، على ملعب "أماهورو" بالعاصمة كيغالي، لحساب الجولة السابعة من الدوري الرواندي. وصدم "الموج الأزرق" جماهيره بتلقي الهزيمة الأسوأ له هذا الموسم، وذلك بعد ساعات قليلة من تأهله إلى مرحلة مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا بأرقام قياسية، حيث احتفظ بسجله خاليا من الهزائم في 4 مباريات بالدورين التمهيديين، ودون أن تستقبل شباكه أي هدف. أداء باهت من الهلال السوداني أمام مارين أنهى الهلال شوط المباراة الأول متأخرا بهدف، قبل أن يتلقى هدفين في الشوط الثاني، وسط تراجع حاد في مستوى نجومه المحليين والمحترفين، في مشهد غير معهود للفريق الذي تألق خلال المواسم الأخيرة، ليتجرع الفريق بهذه النتيجة خسارة ثقيلة في ثاني مبارياته بالدوري الرواندي. وشهدت المباراة حدثا لافتا بعودة مهاجم الفريق أداما كوليبالي بعد فترة غياب دامت أشهرا طويلة، بسبب إصابة في الأربطة المتقاطعة. اقرأ أيضًا رامي كمال: نحترم بيراميدز ولا نخشاه.. والهلال قادر على المنافسة نتائج قرعة دوري أبطال أفريقيا 2027 والمجموعات واستعان مدرب الفريق جوزيف زينباور بعدد من عناصره الأساسية إلى جانب لاعبين بدلاء، لكنهم فشلوا جميعا في تقديم أداء مقنع، كما لم تجد التغييرات التي أجراها في الشوط الثاني نفعا في تحسين الأداء أو تعديل النتيجة؛ ليتجرع الفريق الخسارة، مما أثار الشكوك حول مستوى البدلاء مقارنة بتألق العناصر الأساسية. ويواجه رفاق القائد محمد عبد الرحمن روزنامة مزدحمة خلال شهري أكتوبر ونوفمبر، تتضمن مباريات قوية في الدوري الرواندي، تزامنا مع استعداد الفريق لبدء مشواره في الدوري السوداني بالفريق الرديف، إضافة إلى انطلاقته في دور المجموعات لدوري أبطال أفريقيا، في أحد أيام 27 أو 28 أو 29 نوفمبر المقبل. النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية لتصلك آخر أخبار الرياضة اشترك معنا دول كرة القدم الأخبار
